summary: Analyzes the solutions proposed for hosts to learn whether IPv6 addresses are being synthesized and which NAT64 prefix and format are used. It concludes by recommending standardization of the approach based on heuristic discovery.

eli5.summary: Several ideas were compared for how a device can find out about a helper. The report picks the one where the device figures it out itself.

questions: how do hosts learn the nat64 prefix
subtitle: Analyzing ways for hosts to discover IPv6 prefixes used for network translation.

tldr.problem: In networks using NAT64 to translate between IPv4 and IPv6, hosts and applications need to know whether an IPv6 address is synthesized from IPv4, and what the NAT64 prefix is, in order to avoid the translator when direct communication is possible or to perform their own address synthesis.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes nine different solution approaches—including DNS queries, DNS extensions, DHCP options, router advertisements, STUN, and access-technology-specific methods—evaluating each against five requirements issues.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends standardizing the heuristic discovery method based on DNS queries to well-known names, as it requires minimal changes to networks and hosts, is backward-compatible, and can be deployed without explicit network support.

today: RFC 7051 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. Its recommended heuristic discovery method was standardized in RFC 7050, which specifies the well-known name and heuristic algorithm for NAT64 prefix discovery.

sections.title: The NAT64 Discovery Problem
sections.content:
NAT64 is a protocol that translates IPv6 packets to IPv4 and vice versa, allowing IPv6-only hosts and applications to reach IPv4-only services. DNS64 is a companion mechanism that synthesizes IPv6 addresses from IPv4 addresses returned by DNS. For these mechanisms to work well, hosts and applications need to know: (1) whether an IPv6 address is synthesized or native, and (2) what IPv6 prefix was used for the synthesis (the Network-Specific Prefix, or NSP, or the Well-Known Prefix, WKP).

Without this information, dual-stack hosts cannot avoid using NAT64 when native IPv4 is available, and applications that must synthesize IPv6 addresses from IPv4 literals in URIs or other data cannot do so.
sections.eli5: When devices need to send messages through both old and new address systems, they need to know: is this address a fake one? And what number was added to create the fake?

sections.title: Use Cases for NAT64 Awareness
sections.content: Hosts need to learn the NAT64 prefix for several important uses. Hosts performing DNSSEC validation locally cannot validate synthetic AAAA records without knowing the NSP and performing DNS64 locally. Applications that encounter IPv4 address literals in protocols like Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP), or in web pages need to synthesize IPv6 addresses to reach those destinations through NAT64. Hosts can also update address selection preferences to prefer native IPv4 or IPv6 over translated addresses, improving connection success rates. A device detecting it is talking through NAT64 can avoid passing synthesized addresses as referrals to parties outside the translation domain.
sections.eli5: Some programs need to check signatures on messages. Some programs find old-style numbers in messages and need new-style numbers instead. Devices want to choose the fastest path through the helpers.

sections.title: Five Key Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five core issues that any solution must consider: Issue #1: distinguishing synthesized from real IPv6 addresses. Issue #2: learning the NSP needed for local IPv6 address synthesis. Issue #3: learning the NSP on hosts that do not implement DNS (a rare case). Issue #4: supporting changes to the NSP over time, such as when a host moves to a new network or the network administrator changes the prefix. Issue #5: supporting multiple NSPs in the same network for load-balancing purposes.

Most solutions address Issues #1 and #2 well; Issue #3 is considered rare; and Issues #4 and #5 are handled in different ways by different proposals.
sections.eli5: Can the device tell if an address is made up? Can it learn the magic number? What if the device has no internet directory? What if the magic number changes? What if the network uses many magic numbers at once?

sections.title: Nine Solution Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC analyzes nine distinct solution approaches: (1) DNS query for a well-known name, where hosts query DNS for a known IPv4-only domain and extract the NSP from the synthesized response. (2) EDNS0 options, where DNS servers add metadata to responses. (3) EDNS0 flags, an alternative EDNS0 approach. (4) A64 DNS records, a new DNS record type for synthesized addresses. (5) DNS TXT and U-NAPTR records, using existing DNS mechanisms. (6) DHCPv6 options, where the DHCPv6 server provides the prefix during host configuration. (7) Router Advertisement options, where routers announce the prefix. (8) STUN-based discovery, using application-layer NAT-detection protocols. (9) Access-technology-specific methods, using 3GPP or similar link-layer signaling.

Each approach has trade-offs in complexity, deployment requirements, impact on hosts and networks, and support for the five requirements issues.
sections.eli5: Nine different ways to solve this were tried: ask the internet directory, add extra information to directory answers, create a new directory entry type, ask a configuration server, ask a router, ask a NAT-finding service, or tell the device during network connection.

sections.title: Recommended Solution: Heuristic Discovery
sections.content:
The RFC recommends standardizing the heuristic discovery method based on DNS queries to well-known names. A host sends a DNS query for an AAAA record (an IPv6 address) of a well-known IPv4-only Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN). If the host receives a negative reply, no NAT64 is present. If it receives a synthetic IPv6 address, the host can extract the NSP by examining the synthesized address: it 'subtracts' the known IPv4 address from the response to determine the NSP.

This approach wins because it requires minimal host and network changes, works without explicit network support, is backward-compatible, does not require new standards (DNS already supports it), and can be deployed and updated without operational overhead. It addresses the most important issues (#1 and #2) and is the only method deployable without any network involvement.
sections.eli5: Ask the directory for a fake address that should not exist. The answer will show you the magic number. This works everywhere, needs no special setup, and old systems ignore it.

sections.title: Security and Spoofing Risks
sections.content: The main security risk is that an attacker could forge DNS responses or man-in-the-middle the DNS exchange, allowing them to inject a false NSP and redirect traffic or cause a denial-of-service. However, if an attacker can already modify DNS responses, they have many other ways to attack; a false NSP is just one more capability. An application-layer approach like STUN is vulnerable to rogue STUN servers. DHCPv6 and Router Advertisement approaches are vulnerable to rogue servers unless secured with DHCPv6 authentication or Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND). The DNS-based approach is as secure as the method used to configure the DNS server addresses on the host: if the host cannot trust DHCP to learn DNS servers, it cannot trust those DNS servers unless DNSSEC validation is used.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could lie about the magic number if they control the internet directory. They could also lie about the directory's address. Using signatures on directory answers (DNSSEC) makes lying harder.
